strengths: First theoretical guarantees for Bayesian deep functional models with rigorous approximation error bounds, posterior consistency, and region selection consistency (Theorems 5.4, 5.7, 5.9)
Well-motivated methodology: spike-and-slab priors on first layer elegantly exploit B-spline locality to enable interpretable region selection while maintaining nonlinear expressiveness

Comprehensive experimental validation: systematic simulations (8 scenarios), four diverse real datasets with detailed preprocessing, and consistent improvements especially under nonlinearity and low SNR
Principled algorithm design with clear three-step inference (MAP fitting → plug-in PIPs → region mapping) and code/data reproducibility
Addresses genuine gap in functional data analysis literature between classical linear methods and black-box deep learning approaches
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical assumptions specify precise hyperparameter rates (Assumption 5.5) but practice uses fixed values (λₙ=10⁻⁵) without sensitivity analysis or justification; theoretically-prescribed depth scaling (Hₙ ≍ min{J_n^(αβ/2), sₙ}) not addressed
Restrictive theoretical assumptions (Assumption 5.2: Ω* must be finite union of intervals; proportional sparsity sₙ ≍ Jₙ) not validated empirically; consequences of violations unexplored

Region identification precision is mediocre for intended applications: ECG F1=0.634 with precision=0.464 (high false positives); Tecator F1=0.339 with precision=0.204; insufficient for clinical interpretability claims

Bayesian framing oversold: uses MAP estimation with plug-in PIPs rather than full posterior inference; claims about 'uncertainty quantification' limited to feature-level PIPs, not predictive intervals; posterior contraction theorem established but never empirically verified; 5-run averaging is pragmatic but ad-hoc

Missing statistical testing: Tables 1-2 report point estimates only without error bars or significance tests; some improvements are modest (Tecator 2.138 vs 2.217/2.567/2.691) and potentially within noise; no comparison of statistical significance across runs

strengths: Clear motivation bridging functional data analysis and deep learning with concrete applications
Comprehensive theoretical analysis providing approximation bounds, posterior consistency, and region selection consistency guarantees
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple simulation scenarios and real datasets with systematic variation of problem characteristics
Well-documented reproducible work with provided code and detailed hyperparameter specifications
Effective visualization of methodology and interpretable posterior inclusion probability outputs
weaknesses: Limited novelty: method straightforwardly combines existing techniques (B-splines, DNNs, spike-and-slab priors, group sparsity) without substantial innovation
Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical rates depend on unknown smoothness parameters (αβ, αg); complex conditions difficult to verify; no guidance on selecting Jn, Hn in practice
Restrictive single-index model assumption fundamentally limits applicability; limited investigation of when assumption is violated or diagnostic tools for model adequacy
Marginal empirical improvements: RMSE gains typically <5-10%; region identification improvements inconsistent; simulations inherently favor proposed method through structural assumptions
Unfair experimental comparisons: baselines (FNN, AdaFNN) lack equal modeling capacity; no statistical significance testing; weak deep learning comparisons
Underutilized Bayesian framework: relies on MAP point estimates rather than principled posterior inference; no credible regions or uncertainty quantification on regions
Spike-and-slab hyperparameter selection lacks guidance; network architecture choices not well justified; sensitivity analysis absent; threshold τ=1/2 for region selection is arbitrary
Real data analysis limited: ECG/Tecator validation uses coarse silver-standard regions; results largely confirm known clinical/scientific knowledge rather than discovering novel signals

strengths: Addresses important problem combining nonlinearity with local sparsity in functional data, with compelling real-world motivation (ECG, neuroimaging).
Novel integration of B-spline expansions, Bayesian DNNs, and structured spike-and-slab priors for interpretable region selection.
Strong theoretical contributions: approximation error bounds (Theorem 5.4), posterior consistency (Theorem 5.7), and selection consistency (Theorem 5.9) with clear assumptions.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: diverse simulations varying multiple factors, four real datasets, multiple baselines, and both prediction and region identification metrics.
Excellent reproducibility: detailed algorithms, hyperparameter specifications, promised code, dataset links, and preprocessing details.
Clear presentation of motivation, methodology, and results with informative visualizations including PIP plots demonstrating interpretability.
weaknesses: Significant gap between Bayesian framing and practical use: MAP estimation rather than full Bayesian inference; plug-in PIPs are asymptotic approximations with unclear finite-sample reliability; multiple random restarts (R=5) suggest optimization challenges.
Region identification precision is consistently low (ECG=0.464, Tecator=0.204) despite high recall, severely limiting interpretability utility—the key motivation for region selection.

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 5.7 requires specific Hₙ-sₙ relationships and hyperparameter rates (Assumption 5.5) that differ substantially from practical defaults; Assumption 5.8 (identifiability) is abstract and hard to verify.
Single-index model assumption (Eq. 1) is restrictive; no discussion of robustness when assumption is violated or guidance on model validation.
Prediction improvements are often modest (RMSE differences <5%) and sometimes marginal (Table 2), questioning whether methodological complexity is justified.

Practical considerations largely unaddressed: no computational cost analysis, no failure mode discussion, limited guidance on hyperparameter selection (Jₙ, network architecture) beyond defaults, scalability to high-dimensional functional inputs unclear.

Region evaluation limitations: only silver-standard annotations (not gold-standard) for ECG/Tecator; no region metrics for Bike/IHPC; limited comparison with methods designed for region selection (FNN, AdaFNN don't perform selection).
Algorithm 1 (critical for reproducibility) relegated to appendix; hyperparameter sensitivity analysis absent; no honest discussion of method limitations and when it is/isn't recommended.

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First Bayesian deep functional model with rigorous guarantees including approximation error bounds, posterior consistency, and selection consistency (Theorems 5.4, 5.7, 5.9)
Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive simulations varying β(t) complexity, link functions, SNR levels, and robustness checks (low SNR, model misspecification, non-Gaussian errors)
Well-motivated methodological design: structured spike-and-slab priors on first layer elegantly connect spline feature selection to functional region identification
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithms, extensive appendices with sensitivity analyses, cross-seed stability studies, and promised code/data availability
Addresses practical problems: real applications on ECG (QRS duration), spectroscopy (water content), and energy prediction demonstrate relevance
Interpretable region selection with uncertainty quantification via posterior inclusion probabilities, balancing recall-precision better than baselines
weaknesses: Weak identifiability condition (Assumption 5.8): violated under collinearity (acknowledged by authors), reinterpreted as 'predictive sparse representative' weakening theoretical guarantees. Real data precision of 0.2-0.5 (Tables 1-2) suggests collinearity common

Gap between theory and practice: theoretical analysis assumes single-index model but practical DNN is more flexible; while paper argues DNN recovers truth, this connection lacks rigor and direct guarantees

Inference via MAP approximation: uses plug-in PIPs from point estimates rather than full posterior sampling. Limited empirical validation of this approximation; no posterior credible intervals or posterior predictive distributions provided

Highly restrictive scope: framework handles only single functional predictor with single projection direction; extension to multiple functional inputs is future work but significantly limits applicability
B-spline dependency creates unresolvable bias-resolution tradeoff; Jn selection via evidence-based criterion achieves only 44% top-3 and 73% within-15% of oracle (Table 3)
Computational cost: ~674 seconds (IHPC) is 6.5× slower than SLoS and comparable to BFRS; scalability to high-dimensional functional data (Jn>500) unclear

Limited precision metrics: perfect recall (1.0) on ECG/Tecator with low precision suggests either ground truth poorly defined or method selects too broadly; extended regions (Figure 5) lack external clinical validation

Insufficient guidance on practical applicability: no diagnostics to detect when Assumption 5.8 fails, limited discussion of failure modes, sparse practical guidance for practitioners on method selection

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap in functional data analysis with interpretable region selection capability
Comprehensive theoretical treatment with three nontrivial results (approximation bounds, posterior consistency, selection consistency) that appear technically sound
Rigorous experimental evaluation with extensive simulations, multiple real datasets, and careful sensitivity analyses across hyperparameters
Honest discussion of limitations including B-spline dependence, single predictor restriction, and interpretation issues with collinear data
Excellent reproducibility with detailed specifications, algorithm descriptions, and computational cost analysis
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (B-spline expansions, spike-and-slab priors, DNNs) rather than introducing fundamental innovation

Assumption 5.8 (identifiability) is problematic: essentially requires that only the true sparse structure achieves the contraction rate, excludes correlation-equivalent solutions, and is unverifiable in practice with correlated functional data

Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical results derive properties of true posterior inclusion probabilities, but practice uses MAP-based plug-in PIPs acknowledged only as 'approximate selection scores' without rigorous justification
Real data results show weak region selection: extremely low precision (0.204-0.464) with substantially over-inclusive selected regions that overshoot silver-standard intervals
Fragile hyperparameter selection: evidence-based Jn choice identifies oracle only 17.6% of the time (44.1% in top-3); strong sensitivity to Jn but minimal practical guidance
Severely limited scope restricted to single functional predictor; extension to multiple functional inputs left as future work despite being essential for most applications
Simulation bias: functional covariates generated from same basis family (cosine) as modeling basis (B-splines), potentially favoring the proposed method
Weak baseline comparisons: FNN and AdaFNN don't perform region selection (unfair comparison); advantages over true competitors (cFuSIM, BFRS, SLoS) are modest on simulations and unclear on real data
Computational overhead not justified: 6.5× slower than simpler methods (673s vs 104s on IHPC); scalability to larger problems not discussed

Incomplete sensitivity analysis: only Jn explored; B-spline degree, knot placement, and network architecture (64-64-64-1) chosen without ablations; Theorem 5.4 constructs L1≍1 but practice uses L1=64 without explaining relevance

strengths: First theoretical guarantees for Bayesian deep functional models: rigorous approximation error bounds, posterior consistency, and selection consistency with complete proofs
Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap between linear interpretable methods and nonlinear black-box approaches; excellent ECG application motivation
Methodologically elegant: spike-and-slab priors on first-layer weight columns combined with flexible deeper layers; clever integration of B-spline localization with DNN flexibility

Comprehensive experimental validation: 24 simulation scenarios with 100 replicates each, 4 real-world datasets, 5 baselines, extensive supplementary analysis including robustness to model misspecification and heavy-tailed errors

Strong empirical results: consistent superiority under nonlinear relationships; better recall-precision balance than baselines; posterior inclusion probabilities provide interpretable uncertainty quantification
Excellent reproducibility: detailed algorithm, hyperparameter specifications, runtime analysis, stability assessment (Appendix A.7), extensive supplementary materials promised to be available

Honest treatment of limitations: clearly acknowledged constraints on single functional predictor, single projection direction, B-spline dependency, and appropriately discussed when assumptions may fail
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Assumptions 5.5-5.6 specify complex hyperparameter rates depending on unknown problem-dependent quantities; practical algorithm uses fixed defaults not tuned to theoretical requirements; no empirical validation that theoretical contraction rates manifest in finite samples

Critical B-spline resolution dependency: choice of J_n requires careful tuning; evidence-based selection achieves only 44.1% top-3 in candidate set and 73.5% within 15% of oracle F1; no principled solution beyond validation set; larger J_n leads to region fragmentation

Modest real-data region selection quality: precision remains low (ECG 0.464, Tecator 0.204) despite high recall; selected regions wider than silver-standard annotations; clinical validation that identified regions are actionable missing; region interpretation depends on domain knowledge

Restrictive model scope: single functional predictor assumption; single projection direction per region; cannot extend directly to multiple functional inputs or classification problems; while honestly acknowledged, significantly limits applicability

Identifiability assumption (5.8) can be violated under strong collinearity: structural difference condition ρ_n(4ε_n) → 0 may not hold; paper acknowledges this but leaves unclear when assumption holds in practice

MAP-based inference not fully justified: cited literature supports MAP PIPs but exact full Bayesian posterior marginals would be preferable; computational cost/benefit analysis of MAP vs. full sampling missing; stability analysis (Appendix A.7) limited to fixed scenarios
Simulation data generated from assumed single-index model: validates method within model class but does not challenge assumptions; robustness experiments (FGAM, heavy-tailed) relegated to appendices
